p.src: Now, after the heroes of Liangshan Marsh had twice defeated Tong Guan, Song Jiang and Wu Yong discussed the need to send someone to the Eastern Capital to discover the true state of affairs and report back to the mountain, so that they might prepare their troops and horses for battle in advance. Before they had finished speaking, Dai Zong, the Magic Traveller, said, “I am willing to go.” Song Jiang said, “Brother, we owe much to you alone for gathering military intelligence. Though you are well able to make the journey, it would be best to have someone accompany and assist you.” Li Kui promptly said, “I will go along and help our elder brother.” Song Jiang laughed. “And you are the Black Whirlwind who never causes trouble!” Li Kui said, “This time I simply will not cause any trouble.” Song Jiang shouted him back, then asked the others, “Which brother dares make this journey?” Liu Tang, the Red-Haired Devil, reported, “How would it be if I accompanied Elder Brother Dai Zong?” Song Jiang was delighted. “Excellent!” That very day, the two men packed their travelling gear and descended the mountain.

p.src: Leaving aside Dai Zong and Liu Tang as they went to the Eastern Capital to gather news, Tong Guan and Bi Sheng collected more than forty thousand remnants of their defeated forces along the road and eventually reached the capital. On the way, they ordered the various commanders to lead their own troops back to their camps, and entered the city with only the Imperial Camp forces. Tong Guan removed his military dress and armour and went directly to Grand Marshal Gao’s residence to confer with him. When the two had met and exchanged the proper courtesies, Gao invited Tong Guan into a secluded rear hall, where they sat down. Tong Guan related everything: how he had suffered crushing defeats in two battles, losing the officers of all eight columns and great numbers of troops and horses, and how Feng Mei had also been captured alive; he asked what could possibly be done. Grand Marshal Gao said, “Grand Councillor, do not distress yourself. We need only conceal this matter from His Present Majesty. Who would dare submit a reckless memorial about it? You and I shall report to the Grand Preceptor and devise a solution.” Tong Guan and Gao Qiu mounted their horses and went directly to Grand Preceptor Cai’s residence. Cai Jing had already been informed that Privy Commissioner Tong had returned and surmised that he had been defeated. When he heard that Gao Qiu had come with him, he ordered them admitted to his study for an audience. Tong Guan bowed to the Grand Preceptor, tears pouring down like rain. Cai Jing said, “Do not distress yourself. I already know all about your loss of troops and horses.” Gao Qiu said, “The bandits dwell in a marsh, and no campaign against them can advance without boats. The Privy Commissioner attacked with cavalry and infantry alone; that is why he was defeated and fell victim to the bandits’ cunning stratagem.” When Tong Guan had recounted the loss of his soldiers and the defeat of his army, Cai Jing said, “You have lost so many troops and horses, consumed so much money and grain, and lost the officers of eight whole columns besides. How could we dare let His Majesty learn of this?” Tong Guan bowed again. “I beg the Grand Preceptor to cover this up and save my life!” Cai Jing said, “Tomorrow we shall merely report that the weather was fiercely hot and the soldiers could not endure the climate, so the campaign was suspended and the troops temporarily withdrawn. But suppose His Majesty grows furious and says, ‘If such a grave threat at the very heart of the realm is not destroyed, it will surely bring disaster in the future.’ If that happens, how will you gentlemen answer?” Gao Qiu said, “This is no idle boast: if the Grand Preceptor will sponsor me to lead an army there in person, I can pacify the place with a single beat of the war drum.” Cai Jing said, “If the Grand Marshal is willing to go in person, nothing could be better. Tomorrow I shall memorialize the throne and recommend you as commander.” Gao Qiu further reported, “There is only one condition: we must obtain an imperial decree granting me discretion to mobilize the army and to procure vessels as needed—whether by requisitioning existing government and civilian boats, or by purchasing timber at official expense to build warships. Only by advancing over land and water together, with ships and cavalry moving in concert, can success be assured within a definite time.” Cai Jing said, “That is easily arranged.” While they were speaking, a gatekeeper reported, “Feng Mei has returned.” Tong Guan was overjoyed. The Grand Preceptor ordered Feng Mei brought in and questioned him about what had happened. After bowing, Feng Mei explained that whenever Song Jiang captured anyone alive and took him up the mountain, he released every one of them without harm, even giving them travelling expenses and ordering them to return home; that was how this junior officer had been able to appear before the Grand Preceptor again. Gao Qiu said, “This is a cunning ruse by the bandits, deliberately intended to insult our state. Henceforth I shall not levy nearby troops, but go directly to Shandong and Hebei to select capable men to accompany me.” Cai Jing said, “Since our plan is settled, we shall meet in the palace tomorrow and present it to the Emperor in person.” They then returned to their respective residences.

p.src: At the third watch-mark of the fifth watch the next morning, they all assembled in the chamber where officials awaited the court session. When the court drums sounded, the officials arranged themselves by rank and precedence on either side of the vermilion courtyard. After completing their bows, ceremonial dances, and salutations, the civil and military officials divided into their respective ranks below the jade steps. Grand Preceptor Cai stepped from the ranks and memorialized: “Recently, Privy Commissioner Tong Guan was sent to command a great army against the bandits of Liangshan Marsh. Of late, however, the fierce heat has prevented the troops and horses from adapting to the climate. Moreover, the bandits dwell amid lakes and marshes, where it is impossible to advance without boats; cavalry and infantry cannot make rapid progress. The campaign has therefore been suspended for the moment, and the forces have returned to their camps to rest while awaiting a further imperial command.” The Emperor said, “In such fierce heat, they cannot go out again!” Cai Jing memorialized: “Tong Guan may await punishment at the Temple of Supreme Unity. Let another man be appointed commander and sent once more to wage war. I humbly request Your Majesty’s clear decree.” The Emperor said, “These bandits are a grave threat at the very heart of the realm and must be destroyed. Who will share this burden with me?” Gao Qiu stepped from the ranks and memorialized: “Though your humble servant has little ability, I am willing to render the service of a dog or horse and go forth to destroy these bandits. I await Your Majesty’s command.” The Emperor said, “Since you are willing to share my burden, you may select whatever troops and horses you require.” Gao Qiu further memorialized: “Liangshan Marsh extends for more than eight hundred li in every direction, and without the aid of boats we cannot advance. I beg an imperial decree authorizing timber to be felled near Liangshan Marsh and craftsmen to be directed to build vessels, or public funds to be used to purchase civilian boats for the campaign.” The Emperor said, “I entrust the matter to you. Deal with it as you see fit and carry out whatever can be done, but take care not to harm the people.” Gao Qiu memorialized, “How would your humble servant dare do so! I ask only that sufficient time be allowed, so that I may accomplish the task.” The Emperor ordered a brocade robe and golden armour brought forth and bestowed upon Gao Qiu, and another auspicious day was chosen for the army’s departure.

p.src: Now these ten armies were all seasoned, well-trained troops. Moreover, the ten military governors had all begun as men of the greenwood; later they had accepted amnesty and risen to such high offices. Every one of them was a valiant warrior of the finest mettle, and none had won his fame through some trifling feat of the moment. That day the Secretariat fixed a deadline and dispatched ten official orders, requiring all ten armies to reach Jizhou on time; any who were late would be punished according to military law. At Jiankang Prefecture in Jinling there was a naval force whose commanding officer was named Liu Menglong. When he was about to be born, his mother dreamed that a black dragon flew into her belly, and thereafter she conceived and bore him. When he grew up, he became thoroughly skilled in the ways of water. Having distinguished himself while suppressing bandits on the gorge rivers of Western Sichuan, he was promoted to commander-general of the forces. He commanded fifteen thousand naval troops and five hundred warships, guarding the region south of the Yangzi. Grand Marshal Gao ordered this naval force and its ships to come with all speed, traveling by night as well as day, and await his command. He also sent a trusted man named Niu Bangxi, who had risen to the rank of infantry commandant, instructing him to requisition vessels all along the river and throughout every waterway. They were all to assemble at Jizhou, be handed over, and placed in service. Grand Marshal Gao had a great many staff officers under his command, but two among them were especially formidable: one was named Dang Shiying, the other Dang Shixiong. The two were brothers, both then serving as commanding officers, and each possessed valor enough to withstand ten thousand men. Grand Marshal Gao also selected fifteen thousand elite soldiers from the imperial encampment, bringing the combined strength of all the forces to one hundred and thirty thousand. He first sent officials throughout the various regions to supply grain and fodder, arranging for their delivery along the route. For several days Grand Marshal Gao busied himself putting armor and uniforms in order and having banners made, and had not yet set out. A poem bears witness:

p.src: Now Dai Zong and Liu Tang stayed in the Eastern Capital for several days. After learning the full particulars, they hastened back to the stronghold by night and reported the matter. When Song Jiang heard that Grand Marshal Gao was personally leading the expedition and was bringing one hundred and thirty thousand troops from across the realm under ten military governors, he grew alarmed and immediately consulted Wu Yong. Wu Yong said, “Brother, do not worry. I too have long heard the names of these ten military governors. They have rendered much service to the court, but only because in former days they met no worthy opponents; that alone allowed them to display their prowess. Now we have this band of fine brothers, men as fierce as wolves and tigers. Those ten military governors are already men whose day has passed. Why should you fear them, brother? Before their ten armies arrive, let us first give them a fright.” Song Jiang asked, “How will you frighten them, Strategist?” Wu Yong replied, “Their ten armies are all to assemble at Jizhou. We shall first send two of our fiercest fighters near Jizhou to meet the approaching troops and strike them in an opening engagement. That will serve as our message to Gao Qiu.” Song Jiang asked, “Whom should we send?” Wu Yong replied, “Send Zhang Qing, the Featherless Arrow, and Dong Ping, the General of the Twin Spears. Those two can undertake it.” Song Jiang ordered the two generals to take one thousand cavalrymen apiece and patrol toward Jizhou, intercepting and attacking the armies arriving from the various regions. He also assigned the naval chieftains to prepare to seize the ships on the marsh. The chieftains in the stronghold were assigned their duties in advance. No more need be said of that now; what followed will soon be known.

p.src: To return to Grand Marshal Gao: after lingering in the capital for more than twenty days, an imperial edict came down urging him to set the army in motion. Gao Qiu first sent the imperial-camp troops out of the city, then selected more than thirty singers and dancing girls from the Court Entertainment Bureau to accompany the army for his amusement. By the time he sacrificed to the banners, took leave of the emperor, and set out, nearly a month had passed. It was early autumn, and officials great and small had all gathered at the roadside pavilion to bid him farewell. Grand Marshal Gao was fully arrayed in military dress and armor and rode a warhorse with a golden saddle. Before him were five remounts with jade bridles and carved saddles; on either side rode the brothers Dang Shiying and Dang Shixiong; and behind followed numerous palace-command officers, army commanders, jurisdictional officers, defense commissioners, training commissioners, and other attendants. The ranks of troops and horses were marshaled with perfect order. A poem says:

p.src: Meanwhile, the ten armies arrived at Jizhou one after another. Military Governor Wang Wende was leading a force from the Northern Capital and neighboring regions, hurrying toward Jizhou by night as well as day, and was still more than forty li from the prefectural city. That day he urged his men and horses onward until they reached a place called Phoenix-Tail Slope, below which stood a great forest. Just as the vanguard was skirting the woods, a gong suddenly sounded. From behind the forest, at the foot of the hillside, a body of troops wheeled into view, with a general at their head blocking the road. The general wore helmet and armor, with bow bent and arrows ready. Beside his bow case and quiver were planted two small yellow banners, each bearing five golden characters: “Heroic General of the Twin Spears; Gallant Lord of Ten Thousand Households.” In his two hands he held two steel spears. This was Dong Ping, the bravest general on Liangshan Marsh at charging the very front of a battle line, and for that reason he was called “Dong the Headlong Charger.” Dong Ping reined in his warhorse, barred the highway, and shouted, “Whose troops are you? If you do not dismount and submit to bonds at once, what are you waiting for?” Wang Wende checked his horse and laughed aloud. “Even bottles and jars have two ears. Surely you have heard of us ten military governors, who have repeatedly won great merit and whose fame resounds throughout the realm—and of the great general Wang Wende?” Dong Ping laughed loudly and shouted, “So you are the great dunce who has come to be slain by your lord!” Wang Wende flew into a rage on hearing this and cursed, “Traitorous brigand! How dare you insult me!” He spurred his horse, leveled his spear, and charged straight at Dong Ping. Dong Ping raised his twin spears and rode out to meet him. The two generals fought for thirty bouts without either gaining the advantage. Realizing that he could not defeat Dong Ping, Wang Wende shouted, “Let us rest a while, then fight again!” Each returned to his own formation. Wang Wende instructed his troops not to become entangled in battle, but to charge straight through. With Wang Wende in front and the whole army behind, they raised a tremendous battle cry and fought their way through.

u.src: The general wore helmet and armor, with bow bent and arrows ready. Beside his bow case and quiver were planted two small yellow banners, each bearing five golden characters: “Heroic General of the Twin Spears; Gallant Lord of Ten Thousand Households.”
In his two hands he held two steel spears.
This was Dong Ping, the bravest general on Liangshan Marsh at charging the very front of a battle line, and for that reason he was called “Dong the Headlong Charger.”
Dong Ping reined in his warhorse, barred the highway, and shouted, “Whose troops are you?
If you do not dismount and submit to bonds at once, what are you waiting for?”

ja: たいしょうおうふみのり
u.src: Wang Wende checked his horse and laughed aloud. “Even bottles and jars have two ears. Surely you have heard of us ten military governors, who have repeatedly won great merit and whose fame resounds throughout the realm—and of the great general Wang Wende?”
Dong Ping laughed loudly and shouted, “So you are the great dunce who has come to be slain by your lord!”
Wang Wende flew into a rage on hearing this and cursed, “Traitorous brigand! How dare you insult me!”
He spurred his horse, leveled his spear, and charged straight at Dong Ping.
Dong Ping raised his twin spears and rode out to meet him.
The two generals fought for thirty bouts without either gaining the advantage.
Realizing that he could not defeat Dong Ping, Wang Wende shouted, “Let us rest a while, then fight again!”
Each returned to his own formation.
Wang Wende instructed his troops not to become entangled in battle, but to charge straight through.
With Wang Wende in front and the whole army behind, they raised a tremendous battle cry and fought their way through.

p.src: Dong Ping led his troops in pursuit from the rear. Just as they passed the woods and raced onward, another body of troops suddenly charged out ahead. At their head was a mighty general, none other than Zhang Qing, the Featherless Arrow. From horseback he thundered, “Do not flee!” He took a stone in his hand and hurled it, striking straight at Wang Wende’s head. Wang Wende tried urgently to dodge, but the stone struck the crest of his helmet. He bent low over the saddle and fled at a gallop. The two generals came racing after him and were almost upon him when a detachment of troops charged in from the side. When Wang Wende looked, he saw that it was the army of his fellow military governor Yang Wen, arriving together to rescue him. Because of this, Dong Ping and Zhang Qing dared pursue no farther and withdrew.

p.src: The armies from both routes entered Jizhou together and settled there, while Prefect Zhang Shuye received the forces from each route. Within a few days, a report came from the vanguard that Grand Commandant Gao's great army had arrived. The ten military governors went out of the city to welcome him. After they had all paid their respects to the grand commandant, they escorted him into the city and temporarily converted the prefectural offices into his headquarters, where he took up lodging. Grand Commandant Gao issued orders for the armies of all ten routes to encamp outside the city and await the arrival of Liu Menglong's naval force. Then they would advance together. Each of these ten armies established its own camp. They felled timber near the hills and plundered doors and windows from people's homes to build huts and shelters, causing the inhabitants grievous harm. Meanwhile, in his headquarters inside the city, Grand Commandant Gao decided which troops would take the field: those with no silver to pay were invariably put at the head of the patrols and sent into battle; those who had silver remained with the central army and received false reports of unearned merit. Such treacherous abuses were by no means confined to this alone.

p.src: Grand Commandant Gao had been in Jizhou no more than a day or two when Liu Menglong's warships arrived, and Liu came to pay his respects at headquarters. When the formalities were over, Gao Qiu immediately summoned all ten military governors to the hall to devise a sound strategy together. Wang Huan and the others reported, "Grand Commandant, first send the cavalry and infantry to reconnoiter the route and draw the bandits out to battle. Then dispatch the warships by water to raid their lair. With the enemy unable to aid either front, we can capture the whole band!" Grand Commandant Gao accepted their proposal. He thereupon assigned Wang Huan and Xu Jing as vanguard commanders; Wang Wende and Mei Zhan to bring up and secure the rear; Zhang Kai and Yang Wen to the left wing; Han Cunbao and Li Congji to the right wing; and Xiang Yuanzhen and Jing Zhong as supporting commanders for front and rear. Dang Shixiong led three thousand elite soldiers aboard the ships to assist Liu Menglong's naval force and supervise the fighting. All the forces received their orders. After three days of preparation, they invited Grand Commandant Gao to inspect the armies of every route. Grand Commandant Gao personally left the city and inspected them one by one. He then ordered all ranks of the three armies and the naval force to advance together, heading straight for Liangshan Marsh.

Song Jiang and the other chieftains led the great army down the mountain, and before they had gone far, they saw the government troops approaching. The vanguard loosed arrows to secure its position, and the troops on both sides drew up facing each other. Then Vanguard Commander Wang Huan rode out wielding a long spear and shouted fiercely from the saddle, "You wanton brigands and death-defying rustics! Do you know the great general Wang Huan?" As the embroidered banners parted in the opposing formation, Song Jiang himself rode out and greeted Wang Huan, saying, "Military Governor Wang, you are advanced in years and no longer fit to serve the state. Wang Huan flew into a rage at this and cursed, "You are merely a tattoo-faced petty clerk! How dare you resist the armies of Heaven!" p.src: One used the Screen Formation Spear, fierce as a thunderbolt; the other the Level Spear, bold as racing thunder. One wielded the Heavenward Spear, impossible to guard against or evade; the other the Wind-Piercing Spear, impossible to withstand or ward off. This one longed to thrust his spear through the clouds of the highest heaven; that one longed to pierce through the nine-bended Yellow River. One spear was like a python leaving its rocky cave; the other like a dragon leaping from the waves. One spearman was mighty as a tiger devouring a sheep; the other swift and splendid as an eagle swooping upon a hare.

p.src: Wang Huan fought a great battle with Lin Chong for some seventy or eighty bouts, with neither gaining the advantage. Both sides sounded the gongs to withdraw. The two generals broke apart and each returned to his own formation. Military Governor Jing Zhong came to the front, bowed from the saddle, and reported to Grand Commandant Gao, "This humble general wishes to fight a bout with the bandits. I beg Your Excellency's command." Grand Commandant Gao ordered Jing Zhong to ride out and engage the enemy. Behind Song Jiang the horse bells rang, and Huyan Zhuo rode forward to meet him. Jing Zhong wielded a great long-hafted saber and rode a yellow horse. The two generals fought for some twenty bouts, until Huyan Zhuo feigned an opening, deflected the great saber, and smoothly raised his steel whip. With a single backhand stroke he struck Jing Zhong squarely on the head, splattering his brains and forcing his eyeballs from their sockets; Jing Zhong fell dead beneath his horse. Seeing that one of his military governors had fallen, Gao Qiu hastily dispatched Xiang Yuanzhen. Spurring his horse and leveling his spear, Xiang flew out before the lines and shouted, "Which of you grass bandits dares fight me?" From behind Song Jiang, Dong Ping, the "General of the Twin Spears," burst out before the lines to fight Xiang Yuanzhen. Before they had fought ten bouts, Xiang Yuanzhen suddenly reined his horse around and fled with his spear trailing behind him. Dong Ping spurred after him, but Xiang Yuanzhen did not return to his formation; he skirted its flank and fled into the open country. Dong Ping raced after him. Xiang Yuanzhen steadied his spear, took his bow in his left hand, nocked an arrow with his right, drew the bow fully, then twisted around and shot backward. Dong Ping heard the twang of the bowstring and raised a hand to ward off the shaft, but the arrow struck him squarely in the right arm. He dropped his spear, wheeled his horse, and fled. Xiang Yuanzhen slung his bow, took another arrow in hand, and turned to pursue him. When Huyan Zhuo and Lin Chong saw this, they rode out together and rescued Dong Ping, bringing him back to their formation. Grand Commandant Gao ordered the great army into a general melee. Song Jiang first had Dong Ping rescued and sent back up the mountain; the troops behind could not hold the enemy back and scattered in every direction. Grand Commandant Gao pursued them all the way to the water's edge, then dispatched men to coordinate with the ships coming by water.

p.src: Now Liu Menglong and Dang Shixiong deployed their naval forces and sailed steadily into the depths of Liangshan Marsh. Before them stretched a boundless expanse of dense reeds and rushes, completely concealing every inlet and channel. The government ships came on in an unbroken forest of masts and poles, covering more than ten li of water. As they proceeded, a cannon suddenly boomed from the hillside, and small boats darted out from every direction. The soldiers aboard the government ships had already been half afraid; now, seeing themselves deep among such reeds, they all fell into a panic. They were powerless against the small boats lying in ambush among the reeds, which surged out together and cut the main fleet apart. The government ships could not aid one another from front to rear, and more than half the troops abandoned their vessels and fled. Seeing the government ranks thrown into confusion, the heroes of Liangshan Marsh beat their drums as one, drove their boats forward, and charged straight at them. When Liu Menglong and Dang Shixiong hurriedly turned their ships around, they discovered that the shallow channels through which they had come had all been blocked by the Liangshan heroes, who had loaded small boats with brushwood, felled trees from the hills, and packed the passages shut. Their oars and sweeps could no longer move at all. The host of soldiers abandoned their boats and plunged into the water. Liu Menglong stripped off his armor and military garb, scrambled ashore, and escaped along a narrow path. Dang Shixiong, however, refused to abandon his ship and kept ordering the sailors to row toward the deeper channels. They had gone less than two li when three small boats appeared ahead. Aboard them were the three Ruan brothers, each holding a duckweed-leaf spear, and they closed in against the ship's side. All the sailors leaped into the water and fled. Dang Shixiong gripped his iron lance and stood in the bow to engage Ruan Xiao'er. Ruan Xiao'er then leaped into the water, while Ruan Xiaowu and Ruan Xiaoqi pressed in upon Dang Shixiong. Realizing that matters had turned against him, Dang Shixiong threw down his iron lance and also jumped into the water. But Zhang Heng, the Boatman, shot up from beneath the water, seized him by the hair with one hand and gripped him around the waist with the other, then whirled him around and flung him onto the roots of the reeds. More than a dozen underlings had already hidden there. They caught him with grappling hooks and noosed ropes, took him alive, and carried him up to the stronghold at the Marsh.

Truly: At Yinling, the lost commander met the divine crossbow; amid the battle at Red Cliffs, the armies encountered a prodigious wind. How Grand Marshal Gao ultimately escaped will be revealed in the next chapter.
